Calma

One short form checks an abortion patient against every fund they qualify for, so clinics and funds can pledge in minutes instead of days, and a person approves every dollar.

Liza Fuentes

Live demo: calma-zb5j.onrender.com (made-up data; the first visit can take a minute to wake up)

Code and report: github.com/AmarantaUrsula/Calma

Log in as clinic rosa@mesa.example.org, fund sam@desertbloom.example.org or admin admin@calma.example.org, password Vamosestarbien

Patient answers one form on their phone (English or Spanish) → matching rules check the clinic's own fund, then every partner fund → clinic and funds each approve their pledge → the patient sees what's covered and what they still owe → reimbursement is tracked.

The problem

Patients piece together the cost of an abortion one fund at a time, by phone, while the price goes up every week they wait.

What it costsAmount
Median self-pay, first trimester$650
Median self-pay, second trimester$1,000
Total cost with travel, in state$411
Total cost with travel, out of state$1,367
Requests to NNAF's 99 funds in one year254,651
People those funds supported136,880
Money they gave (average pledge $475)$50.7M

Who has it: patients who can't afford care, clinic front desks, and abortion funds that mostly run on volunteers.

How it works today:

  • The patient calls the clinic, then each fund's hotline: voicemails, callbacks, the same personal details every time. No single fund covers the whole cost.
  • Each fund has its own rules (where you live, income, weeks pregnant, age, travel, insurance). Hardly anyone can keep track of a dozen of them.
  • Staff re-enter the same case in spreadsheets, hotline software and email. Rule lists go stale: the earlier pilot kept them in Salesforce, updated by hand.

What it costs: every delay pushes care later, when it costs more. Staff hours go to data entry instead of patients.

Sources: KFF (2017–2023 data); JAMA Network Open; National Network of Abortion Funds (NNAF) 2024 survey; The Nation (2024).

What is new

Existing tools either list funds or track one fund's cases. None checks every fund at once and then runs the pledges.

Closest prior work: the Autonomy pilot with a Planned Parenthood affiliate (same core idea, rules kept by hand in Salesforce, never fully adopted). Calma rebuilds it without Salesforce and adds AI-maintained fund rules, bilingual self-service, travel and state-of-care funds, two-sided partnerships, explained matches ("Income is 113% of poverty line, limit 300%"), and reports you ask for in a sentence.

How the agents work

AI does two narrow jobs. Plain code and people make every decision about money.

Fund Rules Extractor reads a fund's eligibility page and fills in structured rules, copying the exact sentence each came from. Code checks every quote.

Report Builder turns a sentence into report settings. It never sees patient data or numbers; Calma's report engine does the math.

Tools: none, by design. Both jobs are "read this, fill in this form". Fetching, saving and approving stay in ordinary code: cheaper and safer.

Model: gpt-5.6-luna with typed outputs. 46 of 47 rule fields right vs. 47 for the larger gpt-5.6-sol, at 1/32 the cost.

How the agents work · one real run

The extractor read Carolina Abortion Fund's real website for $0.0009, and a person approved the result.

  1. Scheduler: the fund is due for a check (every 60 days).
  2. Fetcher: robots.txt allows it; the page is stripped to 4,101 characters of text. Unchanged pages stop here, at no cost.
  3. Extractor (AI): one call, 2,299 input tokens (1,265 cached), 550 output, 4.8 seconds, $0.00089.
  4. Result: NC and SC; "lives in or gets care in", quoting "We fund callers who either live in North or South Carolina and/or have an appointment in…"; no income limit; no pledge amount published, so it's left for a person to fill in.
  5. Quote checker: every quote is in the page; nothing invented.
  6. Admin compares current and suggested rules side by side, adds the amount, and approves. Saved as a new version, logged under their name.

AI costs about a cent per staff user a month. Patients cost nothing, because screening is plain code.

Averages over 10 fund pages and 8 report requests, from OpenAI's usage figures. *Hosting at 10,000 users is an estimate. Hosting, not AI, is the main cost.

What keeps it cheap

  • No AI in screening, the step that runs for every patient.
  • Unchanged fund pages are detected by a hash and never sent to the AI.
  • The cheapest model that does the job: Luna is 32× cheaper than Sol.
  • Prompt caching: 64% of input tokens cached, cutting each run's cost by 24%.
  • Small inputs: page text is capped, and the Report Builder never receives data.

Did cutting cost hurt quality? Barely. Luna missed 1 of 47 rule fields (Sol: 0), and the quote checker flagged that miss before anyone could approve it. On report requests the two models gave identical answers.

Safety

AI may suggest; tested code and people decide. A prompt-injection attack on a fund page changed nothing.

RiskWhat stops itShown working
Attacks: prompt injection, data leaksInput is treated as data; typed outputs allow only fixed fields; the Report Builder has no patient data to leak; role checks run in code after the AI.Injection test (right); "list every patient's name" returns a count table, no names
Malfunction: invented facts, wrong action, loopsEvery rule needs a quote that code verifies; agents have no tools or write access; a person approves every rule change and pledge; 3–4 model requests per run at most.Invented quote flagged by test; Luna's one real miss flagged
OverspendingEvery call is checked first against 30 per person per hour and 300 per site per day, then logged with its tokens and cost.Tests: a call over the hourly limit is refused; the daily cap stops everyone

Impact

Minutes instead of days for patients, and an estimated 50–75 staff hours a month saved for each clinic and its funds.

A real tester went through the demo with the written guide. Their feedback led to five changes, now live: plain case statuses, approvals sorted first, a clinic reference number, income-limit exceptions for unhoused patients and minors seeking a judicial bypass, and no clinic-fund pledge when the patient's state Medicaid covers abortion.

What's next

Next: a pilot with one clinic and its partner funds, then the security work needed for real patient data.

What doesn't work yet

  • Not ready for real patient data: needs HIPAA agreements with the host and OpenAI, encryption at rest, password reset and two-factor login.
  • No real texts or emails: the clinic copies the patient link by hand.
  • Rules it can't express yet: identity-based eligibility, funds that pay only certain clinics.
  • Can't read PDFs or JavaScript-only fund pages. Many funds don't publish their criteria at all.
  • Spanish not yet reviewed by a native speaker; one tester so far.

With another month

  1. Pilot with one clinic and two or three partner funds; measure minutes per case and pledges per patient against today.
  2. Security: password reset, two-factor login, Postgres with encryption, an outside review.
  3. Send links and status updates by text or email, worded so a lock screen doesn't reveal anything.
  4. New rule types, and optional auto-approval up to a limit.
  5. A tool-using agent that finds each fund's eligibility page or PDF.
  6. A shared statewide intake for a network of funds.
